# Grammar and design

Gray now converts source text into tokens, parses one expression into an AST and prints its hierarchy. It reuses the scanner, Token class, and literal, unary, binary, and grouping classes from previous labs. Printing is implemented by the AST classes \_\_str\_\_() methods. 

Now instead of ambiguous grammar, this grammar shows precedence levels:  
expression → logical\_or ;  
logical\_or → logical\_and ( "or" logical\_and )\* ;  
logical\_and → equality ( "and" equality )\* ;  
equality → comparison ( ( "==" | "\!=" ) comparison )\* ;  
comparison → term ( ( "\>" | "\>=" | "\<" | "\<=" ) term )\* ;  
term → factor ( ( "+" | "-" ) factor )\* ;  
factor → unary ( ( "\*" | "/" ) unary )\* ;  
unary → ( "\!" | "-" ) unary | primary ;  
primary → NUMBER | STRING | "true" | "false" | "null"  
        | "(" expression ")" ;

Here \* outside quotations means zero or more repetitions. Literals include integers, decimals, strings, booleans, and null values. 

| Precedence (lowest to highest) | Operators | Associativity |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Logical OR | or | Left |
| Logical AND | and | Left |
| Equality | \==, \!= | Left |
| Comparison | \<, \<=, \>, \>= | Left |
| Add/Subtract | \+, \- | Left |
| Multiply/divide | \*, / | Left |
| Unary | \!, \- | Right |

Parentheses override normal precedence. Gray follows Lox’s recursive descent approach but has null instead of nil. It also has thse same logical operators from lab2 grammar. Assignment, variables, and statements are outside this expression grammar.   
Each parser method handles one precedence level. A shared binary\_chain() helper repeatedly builds binary nodes on the left, making left associativity. Unary parsing does it on the right. The parser requires EOF and rejects trailing tokens after an expression. Lexical errors prevent parsing. Syntax errors prevent AST printing. Interactive mode is still usable after either error.

# Setup and run

Run these from the repository root:

Run python src/[gray.py](http://gray.py) to enter interactive mode. One expression at each prompt and ctrl+c to exit. 

python test/lab3/test\_parser.py

python src/[gray.py](http://gray.py) test/lab3/precendence.gray

python test/lab3/test\_parser.py \> test/lab3/results.txt 2\>&1

The test script writes the named .gray inputs into test/lab3/ These inputs and the script are in the submission. Valid file will run exit with status 0\. Lexical or syntax errors will exit with status 65\. The test script exits with 0 when all checks pass.

These cases cover every supported operator, literal type, and AST class. The parser checks syntax rather than operand types, so comparisons combined with equality are represented without evaluation or type checking.

# Interactive recovery

This verifies continued use after syntax and lexical errors, plus an exit at EOF.   
Here is the test script:  
1 \+  
4 \+ 5  
@  
6 \* 7

Expected two line 1 errors, no AST for either invalid line, and the valid ASTs (+ 4 5\) and (\* 6 7\) afterwards. 

Actual output:

Test interactive\_recovery  
Source: '1 \+\\n4 \+ 5\\n@\\n6 \* 7\\n'  
Expected two errors, valid ASTs afterward, then EOF exit  
Actual stdout:  
\> \> (+ 4 5\)  
\> \> (\* 6 7\)  
\>   
Exiting REPL...

Actual error output:

\[line 1\] Error at end: Expected an expression (literal, unary operator, or '(').  
\[line 1\] Error: That character isn't valid: '@'.

Result: pass. Exit status 0\. 

# Syntax tree and AST

Syntax tree for expression 1 \+ 2 \* 3:

![][image1]

The program prints (+ 1 ( \* 2 3))

The AST shows a simpler version of the syntax tree. In 1 \+ 2 \* 3, the multiplication stays together inside the addition because multiplication comes first. The printed output (+ 1 ( \* 2 3)) shows the real order. 

# Limitations

Gray now parses and prints expressions but doesn’t execute them or check operand types. Each file or input can only have one expression. Parsing stops at the first syntax error. The next interactive input starts a new parse. All tests passed.
